cues.text: A Young King and a Reforming Pope
By the mid-1070s, the young German king Henry IV stood in escalating conflict with Pope Gregory VII .
Gregory was a determined reformer intent on freeing the Church from lay control over episcopal appointments, known as lay investiture.
Through this practice, kings and nobles had long claimed the right to install bishops and abbots in office.

When Gregory threatened to excommunicate several of Henry's own advisors for continuing simoniacal practices, and pressed the king himself toward compliance with reform, Henry resolved to strike first.
Deposing a Pope
In January 1076, Henry summoned an assembly of German bishops loyal to the crown to Worms .
There, informed — accurately or not — that Gregory intended to depose him, the assembled clergy issued a declaration renouncing their obedience to the pope.
They declared him deposed and unfit for office, citing accusations of misconduct in his own election and abuse of episcopal authority.
Gregory's Response
Gregory VII's reply was swift and total: within weeks he formally excommunicated Henry.
In an unprecedented additional step, he released all of the king's subjects from their oaths of loyalty to him.
This struck directly at Henry's political foundations, since German nobles already restive under his authority now had explicit papal cover to abandon him.
Canossa
The political consequences of Worms and its excommunication proved catastrophic for Henry.
German princes, seizing the opportunity, threatened to depose him unless he secured absolution within a year.
This forced the humbled king to travel across the Alps in the depths of winter to seek Gregory's forgiveness at Canossa .
There, according to tradition, he stood barefoot in the snow for three days as a penitent.
The pope would then receive him back into communion — one of the most vivid and enduring images of the medieval struggle between royal and papal authority.
Legacy
Worms opened the acute phase of what historians call the Investiture Controversy , a conflict over spiritual and temporal power.
It would not find a lasting settlement until the Concordat of Worms in 1122—negotiated, fittingly, in the city where the crisis had first been declared.
Though Henry's humiliation at Canossa proved only a temporary setback, the conflict would continue for decades afterward.

The synod of 1076 remains the opening act of one of the defining confrontations of the entire medieval Church: the moment a king first attempted, and failed, to depose a reforming pope by his own unilateral decree.
